newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian oil shares pin recovery on higher margin.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian oil shares pin recovery on higher margin.

text.p: Nigerian oil marketing firms, whose share prices are currently falling, will only be attractive again if allowed higher profit margins by the authorities, according to industry managers.
The marketers, until recently the toast of the Nigerian stock market, have posted sharp declines in 1996 profits.

While Mobil's 1996 after tax profit fell to 933.7 million naira from 1.2 billion naira in 1995, that of National Oil and Chemical Marketing Company shrank 80 percent to 253.4 million naira in 1996 from 1.2 billion naira in 1995.
Total posted 837.8 million naira as after-tax profit from 1.1 billion naira the previous year.
Agip barely returned a steady profit, rising to 225.1 million naira against 220.1 million naira.
Managers blamed the trend on low profit margins allowed them by state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC).

"The major threat to the continued sustenance of our usual level of profit is the fixed margin on fuels controlled by government which has not been reviewed since October 1994," Total Nigeria's chairman J-J Chateau told its annual general meeting.

Production costs have escalated to 2.90 naira a litre, but the marketers are only allowed 1.30 naira profit from the 11.00 naira a litre pump price. Apart from taxes and NNPC's share, the biggest chunk -- 5.30 naira -- goes to the Petroleum Trust Fund (PTF). This was created in 1994 to invest the results of a four-fold hike in petrol prices in Nigeria's poor infrastructure.
Persistent calls on government by the companies to review their share has not yielded any fruit.
National Oil's chief executive Orlando Ojo was quoted by a local newspaper on Wednesday as saying the future would remain bleak for the sector unless the margin was improved.
"A litre of water sells higher than a litre of petrol," Ojo said.

He laid some of the blame for National's lower profit on a Saudi ban on Nigerian Moslems making the annual pilgrimage to Mecca last year. This resulted in a substantial drop in demand for aviation fuel, of which National is the leading supplier.

Potentially more damaging to the oil firms is a persistent fuel scarcity plaguing OPEC-member Nigeria, analysts said. Commentators blame below-capacity operation of NNPC's refineries and smuggling of products.

"Most fuel stations have been rendered idle in the past few months because of this lingering scarcity of products and this will reflect in their (the companies') 1997 financial statements," said one analyst, warning of even poorer 1997 trading results.
These factors have dampened enthusiasm in the stocks on the trading floor, forcing investors to dump hitherto precious oil company shares in recent days.
Most, except Agip which fell 30 kobo to 19 naira, closed steady at Thursday's trading but traders said they had large chunks to offer.
Analysts said most oil product marketers were diversifying to other businesses to bolster profits. They cited Mobil, which has established a real estate arm to provide luxury housing.
